episodes.176429: A cold front crossed central Pennsylvania during the afternoon of February 21, 2023, preceded by bands of gusty low-topped rain showers and thunderstorms, aided by steep lapse rates and appreciable deep-layer shear. Small (sub-severe) hail was also observed in some locations.
episodes.176797: A broken line of thunderstorms intensified as it raced east-northeast, causing several locally damaging wind events. The storms were associated with a compact 500 mb shortwave trough and related jet streak that raced northeast from the southern Plains.  Within the warm sector of the surface low, a low-topped broken line of thunderstorms advanced northeast across southern Illinois. Unseasonably warm surface temperatures in the lower 70's and surface dew points in the lower 60's contributed to a modest diurnal uptick in intensity related to afternoon heating.

episodes.176879: A robust mid-level short wave with a surface cold front brought scattered severe weather to our region. Severe thunderstorms in NJ developed, aided by a high shear/low CAPE environment. One supercell spawned a tornado.
episodes.177035: Minor flooding occurred along sections of the Ohio River. The flooding was due to a series of frontal passages that brought showers and thunderstorms on ground that was already very moist. The widespread heavy rain event on the 16th was the primary reason for this minor flooding event on the Ohio River.
episodes.177128: Freezing rain developed across portions of northern Illinois during the morning of February 22nd and continued into the early morning of February 23rd with the bulk of the freezing rain falling from mid afternoon through mid evening.  Thousands of tree limbs and hundreds of power lines came down due to the weight of the ice and northeast winds gusting to 35 mph.  Several trees also came down, including one in Arlington Heights that destroyed a detached garage.  At least 210,000 customers lost power and power wasn't fully restored for some customers for several days.  The hardest hit areas were in Lake, MeHenry and northern Cook Counties.  Several roads were closed due to downed power lines and tree limbs.  In some areas, plows were used to clear roads of downed tree limbs.  Ice accumulation amounts ranged from 0.2 to 0.3 inches with locally higher amounts.  Measured ice accumulations included 0.39 inches at DuPage Airport; 0.37 inches at Rockford Airport and 0.17 inches at Chicago Executive Airport in Wheeling. ||A period of light freezing rain developed across the southeast suburbs of Chicago early in the morning of February 22nd with temperatures near freezing.  Temperatures warmed above freezing by mid morning.||Heavy rain fell across east central Illinois in the afternoon and early evening of February 22nd with the heaviest rain across southern Ford and south central Iroquois Counties where localized flooding occurred.  Storm total rainfall amounts included, in Iroquois County, 3.71 inches two miles north northwest of Cissna Park; 3.56 inches one mile south of Cissna Park; 3.51 inches two miles west northwest of Loda; 3.40 inches four miles east northeast of Milford and 3.35 inches four miles east northeast of Buckley.  In Ford County, 3.86 inches in Gibson City; 3.29 inches three miles west northwest of Gibson City; 3.20 inches in Paxton and 2.93 inches four miles west southwest of Melvin.
episodes.177718: An upper level low brought a cold front through South Central Texas which generated thunderstorms. One of these storms produced severe wind gusts.
episodes.177928: Scattered showers and storms developed along a warm front that was along the I-70 corridor. Some of the storms produce large hail.

episodes.177932: Another round of showers and thunderstorms developed along a front that traversed the CWA between mid-morning and evening on February 22nd.  There were numerous reports of damaging winds.

episodes.177973: A warm front draped along the I-72 corridor served as the initial focusing mechanism for convection across central Illinois on February 22nd.  Midday temperatures ranged from the upper 30s north of the boundary in the Peoria area to the lower 70s along and south of I-70.  An upper-level disturbance interacting with the sharp temperature gradient triggered clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms during the late morning that dropped hail up to the size of quarters across portions of Champaign, Douglas, and Edgar counties.  As low pressure and a trailing cold front approached from the west, a line of thunderstorms developed across south-central Illinois during the afternoon.  These storms brought scattered wind damage to locations south of the I-72 corridor.  Further north along and north of the warm front, persistent showers and thunderstorms brought locally heavy rainfall of 3 to 4 inches, including 3.40 at the National Weather Service office in Lincoln in Logan County.  This caused pockets of flash flooding across parts of Logan, Mason, and Menard counties.
episodes.177987: A potent storm system moving over Arizona resulted in very strong winds in excess of 50-60 mph across most of the region on the 22nd, especially during the morning through the afternoon hours.
episodes.178176: Strong gradient winds developed across the Delta region ahead of an approaching cold front on February 22, 2023. Winds gusted to over 50 mph causing some minor damage. A couple of severe storms developed along the cold front during the afternoon hours of February 22, 2023, resulting in some damaging straight-line winds across the Delta.

events.narrative: Gusty rain showers producing winds estimated near 50 mph knocked out power to more than 250 customers in the borough of Blossburg.
Minor flooding on the Ohio River inundated some low-lying woods and fields near the river.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts of 71 mph that were measured by the West Texas Mesonet site southwest of Comstock.
A mesonet station located near Tortilla Flat measured a wind gust of 72 mph as a line of showers and storms quickly moved eastward through the foothills north and east of Phoenix.
Thunderstorm winds tossed a large set of yard furniture at least 20 feet.
Thunderstorm winds peeled part of the roof off of a warehouse near the Gateway Grizzlies stadium.
Several utility poles were snapped along Highway 149 south of Marked Tree.
An outbuilding was overturned and damaged.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree.
A wide swath of damaging winds from St. Jacob eastward through Highland to the county line. Numerous trees, tree limbs, road signs and powerlines were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large trees as well as numerous tree limbs around town.
Straight-line winds damaged the roof of a building at the Malden airport. A small pump station was also damaged a few hundred yards east of the airport.
Power lines were down due to the storm.

A wide swath of wind damage across the northern half of Clinton County. In Saint Rose, shingles were blown off of a home and a machine shed sustained moderate damage.  Some power poles were blown down just southwest of Jamestown. Otherwise, numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

Several large trees were down in the Cape Girardeau area. About 2,500 customers were without power in the Cape Girardeau area. A trained spotter just north of Delta estimated winds gusted to 60 mph. A few limbs were down in that area.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree in town.

Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous limbs and tore some siding off of a house about two miles north of Pocahontas. Just south southeast of Greenville the tin roof of an outbuilding was peeled up and several trees and tree limbs were blown down.
Thunderstorm winds damaged the doors and skylights on a pole barn. Also, several large tree limbs were blown down.
A peak wind gust of 60 mph was measured at the Cape Girardeau airport near Scott City.
Trees were down and limbs were snapped.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs and caused some minor shingle damage to the roof of the house.
The automated weather observation system at the Carbondale airport measured a wind gust to 61 mph. A power pole was leaning on Old Highway 13 a few miles west of Carbondale.
Several roadways had water flowing across them in southern Mason County.
Time estimated via radar.
Straight-line winds ripped a shutter off a home and knocked a few small limbs down.
A tree fell on a house between Wickliffe and Blandville.
Powerlines were blown down.
A few trees were blown down, blocking roads. Two of the trees were in western McCracken County, and another was in the city of Paducah.
A clothes line and part of a metal fence were blown down on Sierra Avenue in Watson.  A carport was blown across the street on Old Watson Road.
Power lines were blown down.
A powerline was blown down on Illinois Route 133 just east of Lovington.
A roof was blown off an old chicken coop.
A wind gust to 60 mph was estimated by a retired NWS employee just north of Mayfield. A tree was down in a yard in the Symsonia area.
Several trailers had roof damage and trees were broken or blown over on the southwest side of Newton.
Water was flowing across State Route 10 in New Holland.
Claypool Road south of Hedgerow School Road was closed due to high water.

Video and photos shared on social media showed flooding in and around Gibson City.  Large portions of North Park were flooded.  Standing water in yards and driveways was shown near 15th Street and Church Street.  A garage was flooded with 1 to 2 feet of water.  Water a few inches deep was flowing across Route 9 near 100 E Road, west of Gibson City.
A photo shared on social media showed flooding of Jones Street at Park Drive.
